newsitem.title: USA: Fed Chairman's hint at higher rates sparks dollar rally.
newsitem.headline: Fed Chairman's hint at higher rates sparks dollar rally.

text.p: Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's warning that interest rates in the United States may head higher to keep inflation in check sparked a sharp rally in the dollar on Wednesday.
During his semiannual report on monetary policy to the Senate Banking Committee, the Fed chairman predicted the economy might grow about two percent this year.
But Greenspan said the Fed may need to raise interest rates to keep inflation under control, and he cautioned that the rally in stocks over the last two years may not be sustainable.

The last time the Fed increased rates was Feb. 1, 1995, when the central bank raised the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans by one-half of a percentage point to six percent to contain inflation.

"He was upbeat on the growth prospects for the U.S. economy and warned that the risks were for higher rates rather than lower rates," said Keith Woodfin, a currency analyst at Foreign Exchange Analytics. "...that bodes well for the dollar."

Higher interest rates help the dollar by making deposits denominated in that currency more attractive to foreign investors. Interest rates in the United States have remained well above those in Japan and Germany, a factor that has already enhanced the dollar's appeal compared to those currencies.

Initially, the dollar slid as Greenspan's remarks sent stock and bond prices tumbling, but the dollar rebounded. Traders said the rally picked up steam as previously set orders to buy dollars were triggered.

The dollar surged on Wednesday more than two pfennigs to 1.6938 German marks and more than one yen to 122.63 Japanese yen. Profit-taking emerged as the dollar neared its highs for the day, causing the currency to retreat, according to traders.
In late New York trading on Wednesday, the dollar settled at 1.6896 marks, up from 1.6718 marks on Tuesday. The dollar fetched 122.06 yen, up from 121.58 yen.
The British pound edged lower to $1.6345 from $1.6355.
The dollar climbed to Canadian $1.3668 from C$1.3598, and rose to 1.4795 Swiss francs from 1.4605 francs.
The next meeting of Fed policy makers is on March 25, with subsequent meetings on May 20 and July 2.
Traders doubted that the Fed would hike rates in March, but they predicted the central bank might tighten monetary policy later in the year.
Greenspan explained that Fed policy makers have taken care not to act prematurely, despite having indicated since last July they are considering raising official interest rates.

"I think March 25 is too early," said Doug Lee, an assistant vice president of foreign exchange at Sakura Bank Ltd. "I would think by mid year we should see a pre-emptive rate hike by the Fed. As we head towards that, the dollar should benefit."
